# Workspace rules for Claude — SaaS MASTER

You are in the **SaaS master workspace**: the storefront source and the
canonical pages every tenant inherits. Same rules as any workspace, with more
reach and more responsibility.

## What you edit here

- The storefront application itself — components, the registry, styles, API
  client. This is the product every tenant runs.
- The canonical page trees on `main`.

A page tree looks like:
```json
{ "schema":"yelo.tree/1", "page":"landing", "root":"page",
  "nodes":{
    "page":{"id":"page","type":"Page","children":["hero","grid"]},
    "hero":{"id":"hero","type":"Hero","props":{"title":"…","subtitle":"…"}},
    "grid":{"id":"grid","type":"StoreGrid","props":{"heading":"…"},
            "bind":{"source":"storefronts"}}
  }}
```

- Change **props** to restyle or reword. Add/remove **children** to change layout.
- Keep `bind.source` values as they are; they map to real backend data.

## Verifying your work — DO NOT use a browser

**Do not install or run Playwright, Puppeteer, Chromium, or any browser
automation.** There is no browser here; attempting it downloads hundreds of MB,
usually fails, and wastes the whole turn.

The preview is already open on the human's screen, beside your terminal, and it
updates as you save. So:

- To check something **rendered**, `curl` the running preview and grep for what
  you expect.
- For anything **visual** — does it look right, is the spacing off, is the
  colour wrong — **describe what you changed and ask the human**. They can see
  it; you cannot. Never claim a change "looks good".

State what you verified (status code, content present) and let the human judge
appearance.

## The servers are already running — do not start or restart them

The dev server and preview are managed by the Studio.

- **Do not** run `npm run dev`, `next dev`, or `next build`.
- **Do not** kill node processes or free ports.
- Saving a file is enough.

If something seems down, say so rather than trying to fix it by restarting.

## Marketplace rules you must never break

These are behaviours, not styling. Anything may be restyled or re-laid-out, but
these must keep working:

- **Closed stores** can't take instant orders. If the store supports scheduled
  or pre-orders, show that path instead of hiding ordering entirely.
- **Unavailable products** must not be addable — the control stays disabled with
  a visible reason.
- **Single-merchant cart** — one store per order. Adding from another store
  prompts to clear the cart.
- **Minimum order** blocks checkout below the threshold.
- **Never invent an API endpoint or backend capability.** The full backend
  reference is in this workspace at **`docs/YELO_API_REFERENCE.md`** — READ IT
  before writing or changing anything that touches data: cart, add-to-cart,
  products, categories, bill/pricing, promos, orders, wallet, auth. It documents
  the real endpoints, their payloads and the exact response keys. If a capability
  isn't in there, say so — do not fabricate a URL or a field name.
- The backend always returns **HTTP 200**; the real status is `body.status`
  (200 = ok). Treat anything else as a failure.

## Design system — the theme lives in `tokens.css`

This workspace's whole palette, type, radii and motion tempo are fourteen CSS
custom properties in **`tokens.css`** at the workspace root. That file is loaded
by the site's root layout, and every piece of site chrome — the header, the nav,
the cart, checkout — is painted from it.

- **A site-wide look change is an edit to `tokens.css`, and nothing else.**
  "Make it warmer", "less green", "softer corners", "calmer motion" — change the
  token, and the change reaches the entire storefront at once.
- **Never hardcode a hex, radius or duration in a component** to achieve a change
  that belongs in a token. That is exactly how a theme ends up applying to one
  section and nowhere else.
- **Do not add a fifteenth token.** Only the documented fourteen are loaded;
  anything else themes nothing. Need more range? Derive from them in your own
  component's CSS.
- **Every site carries light AND dark.** `tokens.css` holds both sets of the
  same fifteen names — `:root` for light, `[data-theme="dark"]` plus a
  `prefers-color-scheme` block for dark. Dark mode is not optional and not an
  inversion: design it, keep the same token names in both, and check contrast in
  each. Remove it only if the person asks.
- Within a component, reuse the derived variables already defined
  (`--ink`, `--paper`, `--card`, `--brand`, `--r`, `--t`) rather than
  reaching past them to the raw tokens.

Do **not** introduce a second colour palette alongside the tokens, a
gradient-heavy hero, or a giant rounded "card" look.

**Every change must stay mobile-responsive.** Think at 390px, 820px and 1280px;
extend the existing media queries rather than bypassing them with fixed widths.

## The storefront shell — the header, hero, cart and checkout are YOURS

The header and nav, the cart drawer, the checkout, the store header, the product cards,
the catalogue, the hero: real component files at **`chrome/<Name>.jsx`** in this
workspace. Your copy is what renders. Nothing to register, no rebuild to ask for.

**THE HEADER IS A DESIGN TASK, NOT A TWEAK.** This workspace deliberately ships with NO
header, hero, catalogue, product card or cart UI of its own. That is not an omission to
work around — there is no generic one to inherit on purpose, because a header built for a
swimming-pool business should have nothing in common with one built for live classes, in
exactly the way their landing pages do not.

So when you build this storefront, **write them**, for THIS business, from the brief:

- `chrome/Header.jsx` — the nav this business actually needs. A classes marketplace
  wants subjects and "my courses"; a pool service wants service areas and a quote
  button. Not a generic store header with the words swapped.
- `chrome/Hero3DSection.jsx`, `chrome/EntrySequence.jsx` — the first impression.
- `chrome/Catalogue.jsx`, `chrome/StoreCard.jsx`, `chrome/StoreHeader.jsx` — how
  this business's offer is browsed and compared.
- `chrome/CartSheet.jsx` — the cart as this business would present it.

If one of those files is absent, CREATE it. Starter versions exist in the shipped app and
are used only so the site still compiles before you have written yours — treat them as
scaffolding to replace, never as a baseline to nudge. Match the design direction and the
page sections you are building, so the shell and the pages read as one product.

**FOUR FILES ARE A BACKEND CONTRACT, AND THOSE ARE SEEDED.** `chrome/CheckoutPanel.jsx`,
`chrome/AuthModal.jsx`, `chrome/OrderReceipt.jsx` and `chrome/BillLines.jsx` are in
this workspace already, carrying the real login, bill, order and payment flows — roughly
120 live API calls between them. **Restyle them as much as you like; keep their API calls
exactly as they are.** Rewriting these from scratch produces a checkout that looks
finished and takes no money, and the merchant discovers that in front of a customer. If
you need the checkout to look completely different, change its markup and styling — not
its fetches, field names or call order.

- **Keep each file's default export.** Keep its imports of the shared
  engine — `../lib/cart` (cart state), `../lib/session`, `../lib/apiPath`,
  `../lib/order` — exactly as they are; that plumbing is how the storefront actually
  works. Restyle and relayout freely; do not fork the engine under `lib/`.
- **The marketplace rules above still hold, even here.** A closed store cannot take an
  instant order; an unavailable product stays un-addable with a visible reason; the cart
  stays single-merchant; the minimum order still blocks checkout; the bill is whatever
  `get_bill_breakdown` returns and the order goes through the real endpoints. You may
  change how all of this LOOKS; you may not remove, fake or bypass what it DOES.
- **Never invent a backend call in chrome.** If a capability is not in
  `docs/YELO_API_REFERENCE.md`, it does not exist — say so rather than fabricate one.

## Design skills — use them for anything visual

Installed design skills are available to you: **impeccable** (the primary —
direction, craft floor, and its sub-commands), **taste-design** and
**emil-design-eng** (layout, typography, spacing, the invisible details),
**apple-design** (physical motion and materials), and the animation set
(**improve-animations**, **find-animation-opportunities**, **review-animations**,
**animation-vocabulary**). When the user asks for a beautiful, professional, or
"best-in-industry" interface — or any non-trivial UI — invoke the relevant skill
BEFORE writing UI: impeccable sets the approach, the others carry it out. Don't
hand-roll design from defaults when these are available.

## Building sections — drag-and-drop compatibility

Pages are laid out visually in the Studio's Design panel, which can only see
components that are **registered** in the component registry.

**Write the best code for the job first.** Where a section fits the component
model naturally, register it — that should cover most sections, and it is what
lets the user edit the page without you. Where making something drag-and-drop
compatible would force a worse design (contorted props, split-up logic), build
it properly and leave it unregistered. Good code beats a marginal editing
affordance; never cripple a component to fit the panel.

One hard constraint: any node `type` used in a **page tree** must exist in the
registry, or the page renders blank and the Studio hides it. Plain sections not
referenced from a tree are unaffected — use those freely.

### The `Custom` node — build ANYTHING, no palette limit

The palette is **not** a ceiling on what this site can be. If the user asks for
something the built-in components can't express — scroll-driven backgrounds,
3D with real lighting, canvas, shaders, a bespoke section — do NOT water the
request down to fit existing components, and do NOT tell them it isn't possible.

Write a real component file in **`components/<Name>.jsx`** in this workspace
(any React is fine: `three`, `@react-three/fiber`, `@react-three/drei`, canvas,
IntersectionObserver, scroll listeners), then reference it from the page tree:

```json
{ "id":"aurora", "type":"Custom",
  "props": { "component":"ScrollAurora", "intensity":0.6, "hue":"teal" } }
```

Give the file a **default export** — `export default function ScrollAurora(props)`.
The registry resolves a named export too, but default is the contract; a
named-only export is what once left a finished section rendering "Preparing…".

`component` is the file's base name. Every other prop is passed straight through
to your component, so expose whatever knobs make sense and the user can still
tweak them in the Design panel. The node stays selectable, re-orderable,
versioned and fork/rebase-able like any other — so you get real code AND
drag-drop, not one at the expense of the other.

Only when a section genuinely maps onto a reusable, well-typed component should
you prefer registering it properly instead. Never contort the design to fit.

For components you do register: keep props flat and typed (strings, numbers,
booleans, enums — never one untyped `config` object), keep them presentational
(data arrives via `bind`, not a fetch inside the component), express layout
variants as a **prop** rather than a forked component, and give every prop a
sensible default.

Rich visuals (3D, scroll or background animation) are welcome. Where natural,
register the outer section so it appears in the layer tree, and expose only the
few knobs a non-technical person would turn — heading, colour, speed, on/off.
Don't surface a camera matrix as a form field, and don't fake editability for
something that won't respond. If a piece genuinely resists the model, leaving it
as a plain component is an acceptable outcome.

Always load heavy visuals lazily, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`, and never
block first paint. A gorgeous hero that janks the preview is a regression.

## Linking — a page's NAME is not its URL

A "Browse bakeries" button once shipped pointing at `/merchant-listing`. That
page exists; its URL is `/stores`. The click produced a web-server 404.

| Page | URL |
|---|---|
| `landing` | `/` |
| `merchant-listing` | `/stores` |
| `checkout` | `/checkout` |
| `store` | `/store/<id>` |
| any page created on request | `/p/<slug>` |

- **Never link to `/<page-name>`.** Use the table.
- **A page created on request lives at `/p/<slug>`, never at `/<slug>`.**
- **Use `next/link` for internal links, not a bare `<a href>`.** The preview is
  served under a path prefix; `<Link>` applies it and a raw anchor does not, so
  a raw internal anchor leaves the site entirely.
- **Never invent a destination.** A change that would create a dead link is
  rejected before it saves.

## Housekeeping

- Never edit `node_modules/`, `.next/`, or lockfiles.
- Don't add dependencies unless asked; prefer what's already installed.
- Work incrementally: one change, verify, report in one or two plain sentences.
- If a command fails, show the real error. Never fabricate success.

## What being master means

- A change here reaches **every tenant**. Tenants tracking a page inherit it
  directly; tenants who forked it get a review prompt. Assume a mistake is
  multiplied by the number of tenants.
- Adding a component to the registry gives every tenant a new building block —
  so register deliberately, with clean props, and add it to the palette for the
  pages where it belongs.
- Removing or renaming a registered type **breaks every tenant page that uses
  it** (those pages render blank and get hidden). Don't rename a live type; add
  the new one and migrate.
- Prefer additive changes. If a change would alter how an existing page looks
  for tenants who never asked for it, say so before making it.

## Boundaries

- Never edit another workspace's directory directly. Tenant pages belong to
  tenants; master changes reach them through the normal update/review flow.
- Don't `git reset`, rebase or rewrite history.
